title: Preparing Congestion Responses from Pre-Crisis Process Logs
abstract: Increasing workload can slow individual operations and increase repeated processing, allowing congestion to persist after a demand surge. We study which dependencies an executable process model must preserve to prepare an effective response from logs recorded before sustained severe overload. The method learns service and routing behavior, compares feasible actions under specified stresses, and fixes a response with an observable activation rule before independent evaluation. In the serial reference experiment, retaining load dependencies reduces backlog and intervention cost by 38.2% relative to static planning and 35.4% relative to predictive component selection. An independent extension covers 288 training datasets across six structures with parallel operations, alternative routes, multiple returns and competing resource constraints. Under routing feedback, the equal-weight comparison reduces no-action-normalized cost by 0.090 with supplied structure; the aggregate advantage disappears with automatically discovered structure. Individual structural improvements do not survive correction for six primary comparisons, and one shared-resource process worsens. The evidence identifies a decision-sensitive modeling problem: dependencies with little predictive value before a crisis can change the preferred response, while structural errors and unsupported extrapolation can negate that benefit. Predictive fit, structural fidelity and the realized quality of the prepared response therefore require separate assessment.

reproducibility_statement: The supplementary research archive contains frozen protocols and code, input checksums, numerical model parameters, original trajectories, all comparator outcomes, and scripts regenerating the analyses and manuscript tables. The primary experiment and later diagnostics are identified separately. The numerical research archive was verified in a relocated copy. The revised manuscript is checked separately for numerical consistency and anonymous PDF metadata. The public anonymous repository link must be supplied separately before submission.
